title: AWS compute services
learningObjective: Identify EC2 instance types, container options (ECS, EKS), serverless compute (Fargate, Lambda), Auto Scaling for elasticity, and load balancers.
foundation: Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers (instances) in many types and sizes.
Containers run on Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS (Kubernetes); AWS Fargate runs them without managing servers. AWS Lambda runs code on events with no servers to manage.
Auto Scaling adds and removes instances with demand (elasticity), and Elastic Load Balancing spreads traffic across them.
engineer: EC2 instance families: general purpose (M, T: balanced, burstable), compute optimized (C: CPU-heavy, batch, gaming, HPC), memory optimized (R, X: in-memory databases, analytics), accelerated computing (P, G, Inf, Trn: ML, graphics), storage optimized (I, D, H: high local I/O, data warehouses), HPC optimized. Also Graviton (Arm) instances.
Containers: Amazon ECS (AWS-native orchestration), Amazon EKS (managed Kubernetes), Amazon ECR (registry). Both run on EC2 or on AWS Fargate (serverless containers).

Serverless: AWS Lambda (event-driven functions, pay per request and duration, max 15-minute runs), AWS Fargate. Other compute: AWS Batch, Amazon Lightsail (simple bundles), AWS Elastic Beanstalk (PaaS-like deployment), AWS Outposts.
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: groups with min/desired/max, scaling policies (target tracking, step, scheduled), health replacement. AWS Auto Scaling spans multiple services.

Elastic Load Balancing: Application Load Balancer (HTTP/HTTPS, layer 7 routing), Network Load Balancer (TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency, layer 4), Gateway Load Balancer (third-party appliances). Load balancers distribute traffic, run health checks and support multi-AZ.

example.title: Picking compute per component
body: The storefront runs on EC2 M-family instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB; the order API runs on ECS with Fargate; image thumbnails are made by Lambda when files land in S3; nightly reports run on AWS Batch.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
configuration.cli:
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --filters Name=instance-type,Values=c7g.* --query 'InstanceTypes[].InstanceType'
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups
aws lambda list-functions

lab.objective: Practise choosing the right compute option.
steps: Pick each requirement, choose an answer and run it.
Read why the best answer fits.
failureScenarios: Choosing by name instead of requirement
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Lambda times out on long jobs.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Fargate, Batch or Step Functions.
Use ELB health checks with Auto Scaling.

comparisons.difference: EC2 ≈ VMs; ECS/EKS ≈ Container Apps/AKS; Lambda ≈ Functions; ALB ≈ Application Gateway; NLB ≈ Load Balancer.

misconceptions.reality: Fargate is a serverless launch type for ECS and EKS.

misconceptions.myth: Auto Scaling is only for scaling out.
misconceptions.reality: It scales in and replaces unhealthy instances too.

architectureDecisions: Prefer serverless (Lambda/Fargate) when it fits; use EC2 for full control.

walkthrough.subtitle: Run one shop app as servers, as containers, then as serverless functions, and scale it.

steps.label: Run the app
steps.title: Where does the code run?
body: Your shop has a website, a checkout service and a job that resizes uploaded images. Each part has different needs.
AWS has several ways to run code. Pick the one that fits each part.

steps.label: EC2
steps.title: Amazon EC2: virtual servers you control
body: EC2 gives you virtual servers (instances). You choose the OS, size and instance family, and you manage the OS.

Families: general purpose (balanced), compute optimized (CPU-heavy, such as batch jobs or game servers), memory optimized (big in-memory databases), storage optimized (high disk I/O), and accelerated computing (GPUs for ML and graphics).

steps.label: Load balancer
steps.title: A load balancer spreads the traffic
body: Elastic Load Balancing receives every request and sends it to a healthy instance, across AZs. It checks the health of each target and stops sending traffic to failed ones.
Users see one address however many servers are behind it.

steps.label: Auto Scaling
steps.title: Auto Scaling adds and removes servers
body: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling keeps the right number of instances: it adds them when CPU or requests rise and removes them when load drops. It also replaces instances that fail.
That is elasticity: capacity that follows demand.

steps.label: Containers
steps.title: Containers: ECS or EKS
body: Containers package an app with everything it needs. Amazon ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator: simple and AWS-native. Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes, which suits teams that already use Kubernetes or need portability.
Both can run containers on EC2 instances you manage, or on Fargate.

steps.label: Fargate
steps.title: Fargate: containers without servers
body: With AWS Fargate you don't provision or patch any instances. You say how much CPU and memory each container needs and pay for that.
Fargate is a serverless way to run ECS or EKS containers.

steps.label: Lambda
steps.title: Lambda: code that runs on events
body: AWS Lambda runs a function when something happens, for example a photo uploaded to S3 or an API request. It scales automatically, and you pay per request and per millisecond of run time, nothing when idle.
That makes it ideal for the image-resize job.

callout.text: Lambda = functions, short tasks (max 15 minutes). Fargate = containers without managing servers. EC2 = full control.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: The right compute for each part
body: Control on one side, less to manage on the other.
recap: EC2: virtual servers; pick the instance family for the workload
ELB: one entry point, health checks, spread across AZs
Fargate: serverless containers; Lambda: event-driven functions
